# Cold read: climb-batch-33 orientation

Read: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md` (the core) and `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-33/orientation/orientation.md`. I opened nothing else. Line numbers below are the orientation's.

The file calls itself "This part" (line 3). Its title and contents match the part that the core lists as `references/revival-changes.md`. The core cites its sections by name: "Numbers" matches, but "Static parameters" is now "Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes". I read it as that part, promoted to the orientation.

## 1. What I would do differently, section by section

Each rule is stated as I understood it from the orientation alone, with its limits.

### Preamble (lines 3-7)

- I would sort every sentence by its marker before I act on it.
  - A `P-N` is a curator decision, and I may cite it as one.
  - A ledger row marks something unsettled. I would never assert it as correct in a plain (non-`XXX`) test. Where the rules decide the case, I would write an `XXX` test of the rules' answer. Where they do not, I would write a plain test of today's behaviour and record it next to the row.
  - "Until the switch-over" is a limit of the compiler's library. I would work around it and not fix it in the prelude.
  - A sentence with no marker is something to build on, but not to cite as a decision.
- Before I call a disagreement a conflict, I would search FACTS and POSITIONS.
- Where the specification's early text and the later type papers disagree, I would expect the papers to win (P-26).
- The Working Draft is `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Appendix I keeps the text that a rule replaced.
- I would not trust old notes, team tests or my training on three points: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.
- Limit: the markers do not sort every sentence (section 2, items 3, 4 and 8).

### Dispatch and overloading (lines 9-24)

- I would allow overloads that differ only in their static-parameter bounds (P-45).
- I would judge every pair on declared domains, and check the Return Type Rule at every instance, not at one.
- With static parameters, I would read exclusion over the whole parameter tuple (P-152). Where both declarations name the same generic type at a position, their static arguments are equal. A pair whose exclusion needs a parameter that nothing ties down is refused on both paths, so I would tie the parameters through a shared position.
- In the exclusion test, the meet of a parameter's bounds stands in for the parameter only where the parameter is a whole parameter type, a tuple element or a member of a union or intersection. Inside a static argument it does not (P-157).
- I would never rely on declaration order. A generic trait method called with an argument outside its bound fails with "Cannot unify".
- I would not change code just to pass walk's load check, and I would not take walk's acceptance as proof. First I would look the case up in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks".
- Functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands. An abstract and a concrete method at the same types in one trait are refused. An object that takes an abstract method from one trait and its body from another must declare the method itself (P-149), unlike in Scala.
- An abstract functional method counts in the Meet Rule. So `h(self)` in a trait `S`, beside a top-level `h(x: String)`, needs a cover of the meet or an exclusion.
- A program's trait with its own functional `+`, `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` needs one of these fixes:
  - `excludes { Number }`;
  - `excludes { HasRank }`, if the trait extends `Number`;
  - declaring the operator in an object instead.

  Otherwise walk refuses the program at load with "fails the Meet Rule". The checker accepts the pair against the library (row 918), so a clean compile does not show that the program loads under walk.

### Traits and objects (lines 26-64)

- **Generic traits.** I would never extend two instantiations of one generic trait. The checker refuses it; walk runs it (row 416). In code for walk, I would not overload on `Tg[\3\]` beside `Tg[\4\]`. I would not copy specification examples marked "Not allowed".
- **`comprises`.** It is about values. Several declarations together can cover a meet. Walk checks only the main component's clauses (row 551).
- **`override`.** I would write `override` only to widen, where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower. To replace a declaration at the same types, I would redeclare it without `override`. Walk refuses a Java-style `override` at load. The checker accepts it (row 653). The code generator refuses every `override` (row 650). So in a program that must compile, I would write no `override` at all.
- **Inherited abstract methods.** An object must cover them, with `comprises` read. Walk checks this only for objects without static parameters (row 665). Where the abstract or a covering method is generic, I would give one body at the full parameter types (row 725).
- **Self-typed traits.** I would return `self` at `X` without a cast. I would avoid a `typecase` with `self` in one arm and another value in another; I would bind `self` to a typed local first (row 1070). If a generic object that lists the trait first fails at class load, I would suspect row 1052. I would not "fix" walk's refusals in the two row-999 cases by changing valid library code.
- **`Index`.**
  - I would write `I extends Index` in the library and in code that runs under walk. Until the switch-over, I would leave it out of compiled programs, because the prelude has no `Index`.
  - I would index with `ZZ32` only; `ZZ64` is no `Index`.
  - `m[i, j]` passes one tuple index. `()` is no `Index`.
  - I would not overload over `Index` beside a tuple of `Index` types without a cover.
  - The checker refuses a tuple expression at an `Index` parameter, but takes one at a parameter `I extends Index` (row 805).
- **Order.** I would compare tuples only where every element type is ordered; an `Unordered` comparison gives `false`. Under the checker, lists need `StandardTotalOrder`, so a `List[\RR64\]` has no `<` there (P-154).
- **Equality.**
  - Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is `SEQV`.
  - I would give every value object that compares by content its own `=`. Without one, equal strings from two computations make `V(s) = V(t)` false.
  - Tuples of four or more elements compare by `SEQV` (row 923).
  - I would never write `≡`, `EQV` or `EQUIV`; I would write `a <-> b`.
  - Equal literals are one object, and `||` of two literals folds into one.
  - The compiler's library differs (row 908).

### Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes (lines 66-85)

- A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not `Nothing`. Under walk, a parameter bounded by itself stays `OPEN`. In the three `Bottom` cases (rows 591, 612, 587), and for a generic call written as an argument (row 705), I would write the static arguments, as `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.
- I would use only the three `where` forms (P-151). The checker reads any other `where` on an `extends` entry as unconditional, without a message. I would not count on a condition being checked at run time (rows 774, 777; the code generator emits no code for the clause). In compiled code, I would avoid functions whose own clause introduces a variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does (row 867).
- I would write each size in one canonical form, because sizes are equal only by written form after numeral arithmetic. I would treat a numeral arm in a `typecase` over sizes as reachable. Size exponents stay at 4096 or below, and none is negative.
- I would use `reflect` and `NatParam` only under walk. In compiled code, I would not pass a value of a trait that lists a type at a `where`-clause size where the listed type is expected (row 307).

### Numbers (lines 87-116)

- **Number types.** I would never extend a number type. A program's own number type goes below `Number`. Walk refuses an object below one of the seven at load. The checker accepts it, and it dies at class load (row 866).
- **Old type names.** I would replace `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` with `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR64`, `ZZ` and `NN64`. A catch-all `typecase` arm is `x: Any =>`, never `x =>`.
- **Numerals.**
  - A numeral converts at a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. Out of range, it is refused there.
  - Anywhere else it takes its default: `ZZ32`, then `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where it does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. The default sticks: after `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused.
  - A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`.
  - I would write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator.
- **A program's own number type.** It takes numerals by a generic coercion, with a `where` bound on the numerals it accepts. It needs a prefix `-` to take `-3`. The coercion runs once per site, and each run of the site reuses the value.
- **`array1` and `array2`.** At a program's own number type they give a plain array, not a `Vector` or a `Matrix`.
- **Tests and the fold.** An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker. So a test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a typed variable operand, as `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`. After the fold, a program's own type takes a constant only through a coercion from the constant's default type (`coerce(q: QQ)` for `10/20`). A negated numeral is the exception: it goes through the type's prefix `-`.
- **Conversion at calls.** Walk converts a value other than a numeral by its run-time type. It does not convert at a declared return type (row 387). A generic call promotes to the narrowest common coercion target. Under walk, tuple and varargs elements are not promoted (rows 395, 511). A numeral can choose a strictly more specific overload through its coercion (P-46), with the departures at rows 1016 and 1017.
- **Integer conversion.** I would convert with the checked getters (`asZZ32` and the others), or with the low-bits functions where wrapping is wanted. For a `ZZ` value, I would write `z.asZZ32`, not `narrow(z)`. On the compiled path, only the subset in row 349 exists.
- **`Number`.** I would never call `asFloat`, or any other method or operator, through `T extends Number`. I would declare the function once for each number type. Across types, `=` works only where a coercion links the two types. Otherwise it is a silent `false`, as for a `ZZ64` against an `RR64`. I would compare such values with `asFloat(x) = y`.
- **Division and powers.**
  - An integer `^` answers its base's type. At a negative exponent it raises, so I would write `2.0^(-1)` or use a `QQ` base.
  - `/` on two integers answers a `QQ`, and `DIV` truncates toward zero.
  - For a float result, I would write `(1.0 s) / n`, and `asFloat` on each `ZZ64` operand.
  - Until the switch-over, the compiled path has no `QQ`.

### Reductions and comprehensions (lines 118-130)

- Where a reduction's type is set by a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable or an assignment, I would write its static argument, as `SUM[\RR64\]...`, in any program for both paths (row 1008). For `BIG MIN_MAX`, I would write both arguments (row 1007).
- As a call's argument, a reduction sums in its body's type on both paths.
- Under walk, an empty `SUM` with no declared type is the integer 0 (row 716).
- In my own reduction without an identity, I would declare `simpleJoin` at `R`, never at `Any` or untyped. I would not copy the team's tests here.

### Implementation limits (lines 132-136)

- I would never write a `Maybe` as an `if` condition.
- I would write every parameter type. A return type may be left out where the api declares it, or where the checker can type the body.

## 2. Passages that would mislead, read two ways, or use a term the core does not give

1. **Line 57, against line 64. `SEQV` "follows the specification on both paths."** Line 64 then says that, until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `=` over `Any` and no `=` on tuples. Its `===` compares strings by `=`, not by identity (row 908). Read literally, line 57 has a worker write a compiled test asserting that two computed equal strings are not `SEQV`, and the test is wrong today. "Both paths" seems to mean "both paths, each on the interpreter's library", but it does not say so. Confidence: high.

2. **Line 24, against line 43. A program's trait with its own functional `+`.** Line 24 says such a trait overlaps the library's array-number `+`, and that walk refuses the program unless the trait excludes `Number` or `HasRank`. Line 43 says that, with `self` read as `T[\X\]` ∩ `X`, the library's array-number `+` is valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. It adds that walk "loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component". A worker with a self-typed program trait that declares `+` cannot tell which passage applies: does it need `excludes { Number }`, or not? Confidence: medium-high.

3. **Line 7. The sentence classes overlap and leave gaps.**
   - Rows 908, 349 and 441/523 sit inside "Until the switch-over" sentences. So each is both "unsettled, write an `XXX` or a plain test" and "a prelude limit, do not fix".
   - Line 89 states prelude limits (rows 1003, 866) without "Until the switch-over". A worker may fix them in the prelude, which line 7 forbids only for the other class.
   - Line 7 says not to fix such limits "in the compiler's prelude". The core says the prelude is three files of the compiler's library. So it is unclear whether a limit in the library's other files may be fixed.

   Confidence: medium.

4. **Line 5. "Each bold rule states the rule of this tree."** Several bold sentences state a behaviour or a difference between the paths, not a rule:
   - line 17: "Walk's load check is not the verdict";
   - line 74: "Only the checker gives...", where walk's side is row 705;
   - line 122: "the two paths fix an unwritten static argument from different places", where the difference is row 1008;
   - line 134: "Walk has no static types".

   For line 122 especially, a worker cannot tell which path holds the rule. An `XXX` test of the rules' answer would need that answer. Confidence: medium.

5. **Line 7. "do not assert it as correct in a plain test", against "a plain test asserts today's behaviour beside the row".** These read as a contradiction until "as correct" and "beside the row" are weighed. A first read takes the first sentence to forbid plain tests of any ledger-row behaviour. Confidence: medium-low.

6. **Lines 116 and 101. The `/` paragraph says that "a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error" because the library "declares `/` only at `RR64`".** By line 101, `7 / 2` folds to the constant `7/2` before the checker. So the error must come from `QQ`'s absence, not from `/`. The example teaches the wrong cause. It also leaves two questions open:
   - Does `s / n` on `ZZ32` variables run at `RR64` on the compiled path, through a coercion, or is it refused?
   - What does an untyped `lr = 1/1000` do on the compiled path? The text says "under walk ... is a `QQ`" and says nothing of the other path.

   This matters for the model program's constants. Confidence: medium.

7. **Line 32. "`override` widens."** The bold rule tells a worker when to write `override`. Only the last clause says that the code generator refuses every `override` (row 650). The net rule for a compiled program, "write no `override`", is never stated, and a worker who follows the bold rule breaks the compile. Line 32 also says "along two paths" (inheritance paths) in a part where "the two paths" otherwise means walk and the compiled path. And it uses "self-typed trait" before line 36 defines it. Confidence: medium (the net rule); low (the wording).

8. **Line 85. "Such a call runs only under walk, also after the switch-over."** There is no row on this sentence, so by line 7 it is a settled rule. The next sentence ties the compiled failure to row 307, which is an open gap. Is walk-only the design, or the gap? Confidence: medium-low.

9. **Line 134. Walk takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition.** This is a departure from the specification and the checker, given without a ledger row, so by line 7 it reads as settled. Confidence: low-medium.

10. **Line 41. "Its test returns `self` at the type that a `comprises` clause lists (row 1070). In that arm, bind `self` at the returned type, as `do r: R = self; r end`."** "Its test" has no clear referent: the row's test? `R` is not defined. It is unclear whether every `typecase` of that shape fails, or only one that returns `self` at a type a `comprises` lists. Confidence: medium.

11. **Line 93, against lines 101 and 112. "A numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type."** Yet `0 = u` is `true` (line 112), and a numeral as the receiver of a dotted call presumably takes its default ("elsewhere", line 97). So is `3.asString` valid or not? The sentence reads as if it is not. Confidence: medium-low.

12. **Line 95, against line 103. "Declared return type" is a place where a numeral converts. Walk "does not" convert at a declared return type (row 387).** The first is about numerals and the second about other values, but nothing marks the difference. A worker may conclude that walk refuses `f(): NN32 = 5`. Confidence: low-medium.

13. **Line 122. "A reduction whose bound does not name its parameter takes its bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit."** The subject is unclear: the checker, walk, or both? And what does not fit what? Confidence: medium.

14. **Line 48. "In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`."** The instruction is unconditional. The paragraph's last sentence takes it back for compiled programs until the switch-over. A worker on the model program, a compiled program, who acts on the first sentence breaks the compile. Confidence: low-medium (the paragraph does correct itself).

15. **Line 5. "Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision."** The core's rule says to cite a source for every claim: the brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source. A skill part is none of these, and the core forbids loading `sources.md` for a task. So what does a worker cite for an unmarked sentence? Confidence: medium-low.

16. **Terms that the core does not give:**
    - "the Meet Rule" (lines 24, 30), cited to `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language". The core says only "a third covers their meet" and names no Meet Rule; "meet" itself is not defined there. Confidence: medium.
    - "instance", meaning instantiation (lines 11, 13, 15, 122). The core says "instantiation", and an OO reader takes "instance" to mean a value. Confidence: low-medium.
    - "extenders" and "main component" (line 30). Confidence: medium.
    - `Unordered`, `StandardPartialOrder` and `StandardTotalOrder` (line 55). These are library names. `StandardPartialOrder` is written without its static argument, `StandardTotalOrder[\E\]` with one. Confidence: low.

17. **Line 11. The `ident` example never says that `Round` extends `Shape`.** Without that, the pair is valid only by exclusion or a meet, and the example does not illustrate P-45. Confidence: low.

18. **Line 19. "So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)`."** The text does not say what walk does, or whether walk's behaviour is a departure. Confidence: low.

## 3. Repair history, or detail that changes no action and prevents no misunderstanding

The file holds almost no repair history: no batch numbers and no accounts of fixes. The candidates below are small.

1. **Line 134. "Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12)."** This is a future plan, and it changes no action today. "Walk has no static types" repeats the core (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). Confidence: medium.

2. **Line 41. "Its test returns `self` at the type that a `comprises` clause lists"; "no test runs such a body".** These describe the test coverage of rows 1070 and 1052, not what a worker should write. The first also blurs the rule (section 2, item 10). Confidence: medium.

3. **Line 89. "The record calls this design route A."** "Route A" is a design-history label. The "tower" half of the sentence prevents a misreading of the record and is worth keeping. "Route A" earns its place only if workers meet it in FACTS. Confidence: low.

4. **Line 114. "Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent... At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523)."** This is behaviour of a prelude due for deletion, and line 7 forbids fixing it. It helps only to diagnose a strange compiled result. Confidence: low.

5. **Line 95. "`t TIMES 10.0`... Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares neither `TIMES` nor `isInfinite`."** It is niche, and it does not say why `TIMES` is used rather than `*`. It changes an action only for a test that needs an infinity. Confidence: low.

6. **Line 93. "The compiler's prelude follows the same design (P-37)."** It changes no action as written. Confidence: low.

7. **Line 32. "An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it."** This is what any reader assumes, so it changes no action. Confidence: low.

<!-- The orientation workflow: consolidate the fortress-repo skill's revival part into a short orientation every worker reads whole, or update it after a landing from the FACTS the landing changed; how to run it and install its result. -->

# The orientation workflow

The `fortress-repo` skill's revival part, `references/revival-changes.md`, becomes the **orientation**: the short account of how revived Fortress departs from the original and from what a model expects, which every worker reads whole (Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`). `orientation.js` writes it, in two modes:

- **consolidate**, once, and again whenever the part has drifted: an outline by the concepts workers use and a table of where each old entry goes (`outline.md`); the writer writes the whole text from them; a preservation check against the table, a cold read with only the skill's core, and the regression quiz; the writer's fix round; a second cold read and the quiz again; a judge.
- **update**, after every landing: the landing's new and changed FACTS and POSITIONS entries pass the admission test (`admission.md`: the wrong default, the correction, the mistake it prevents); the writer rewrites the sections they touch in place, within the budget of 8K to 12K characters; the same checks, fix round, reread and judge.

The writer is a headless Opus stream (`../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`), so its fix round resumes the session that wrote the text. The regression quiz is kept in `regression/` (questions and key), and grows with each update.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/orientation.js',
               args: { mode: 'consolidate', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation', concepts: ['/abs/concepts.md'] } })
    Workflow({ scriptPath: ..., args: { mode: 'update', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation-bN', facts: ['F-261', 'P-153'] } })

## Installing its result

The judge writes `judgement.md` and `queue.md`. The coordinator then has the skill writer (`skill-writer.sh`) install the sections judged "install" into `references/revival-changes.md`, add `sources-mapping.md` to the skill's `references/sources.md`, and, after a consolidation, update the core's line for the part and its description together; then a cold read of the installed part, as `coordinator/references/skill-rewrite.md` says. Held sections keep the old text; their items go to `review-queue.md`.
<!-- The orientation workflow's admission brief, update mode: which findings of a landing earn a place in the orientation. -->

You decide which findings of a landed batch change the `fortress-repo` skill's orientation, in the Fortress revival repository. Change nothing but your report. Commit nothing. Your standard: `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`, "A small change to the existing process" and "Recovered admission rule, workflow runs and transcript search pointers".

Your launch message names the FACTS and POSITIONS entries the landing added or changed. For each (`explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'F-N+'` or `'P-N+'`): does it change what a worker must understand or do? Name the default assumption a worker would hold, the correction for revived Fortress, the consequential mistake it prevents, and the evidence of that mistake (a failure on record, the regression quiz, or the pretraining quiz). If the orientation already states it, or an area part owns it, or no worker would act differently, it is not admitted: say where it belongs instead. Read the skill's current orientation, `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md`, before you decide.

Write `admission.md` in your folder: one row per entry, admitted or not, the reason, and for an admitted one the section it changes. Your structured result: the admitted entries, and a summary.

# Admission: climb batch 33, run 1

An undefined name in a tuple arm still binds on both paths, with no message (row 1064). So under walk `(NoSuchType, ZZ32) =>` takes `("s", 3)`. Compiled, with an `Any` selector, the checker refuses that arm: 'The typecase clause, Pattern at ..., is unreachable.' In their place, write `ZZ32` for `Int`, `ZZ64` for `Long`, `RR64` for `Float`, `ZZ` for `BigNum` and `NN64` for `UnsignedLong`.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/fortress-repo

# Working in the Fortress revival repository

The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**brief**
: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.

**original tree**
: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.

**record**
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**model program**
: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.

**one library**
: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the runtime), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, or a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"), run your test on both paths. `references/compiler.md`, "Natives", says how to test such a class on the compiled path. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
2. Bind each name to its declaration.
3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
4. Fold each expression of numerals alone into one exact value: a numeral, a quotient of two numerals or a boolean (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").
5. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
6. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
7. Mark each call of an overloaded name.

Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.

### The compiled runtime

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).

`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.

### Parallelism and mutable state

Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.

`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A value object is a tuple, `()`, or an object whose declaration, or a trait that it extends, has the `value` modifier, as the library's numbers, characters and booleans do. It has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Nothing refuses a `var` field in a value object, so give it none. Any other object, except a function, is a reference object, like an instance of a Swift class. Each construction makes a new reference object, distinct from all others (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:24-33`).

Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:

- Most data is immutable.
- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").

So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.

Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes, an object's `var` field among them. From the switch-over, it also tracks each array element that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).

An `exit` out of an `atomic` block loses the block's writes, on both paths (ledger row 1039). Set a flag in the block, and exit after the block.

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's: the Return Type Rule. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, but a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's numbers: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion does not change which declaration runs when one already fits. A numeral is the one exception: it can run a more specific declaration that its coercion reaches. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

## The record

The record's main files:

- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.

## When to explore

Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:

- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.

When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.

## Rules for every task

- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).
- Assert every value that matters inside the test, with the harness's own checks (`references/tests-writing.md`), and take the suite's pass or fail as the result. Do not compare the output of a whole run of tests with a saved copy, and do not add expected-output files. The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").
- Take the tree that you start from as passing: its suites passed before it landed. Do not run them to check that. Start with your own failing test.
- Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate, a test or a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it. Run it again only after the code changes. Running a new program is not a repeat.
- Before you investigate a defect, or edit a file of the original tree, look for its rows in the gap ledger, with the queries of `references/records.md`, "Reading the record".
- After your fix, run your own tests. Run a whole suite where `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", asks for it, and nowhere else.
- Set up each Bash call as `references/build-and-caches.md` says, because every call starts a new shell.
- After an edit, take the step that `references/build-and-caches.md` gives for the kind of file that you edited.
- Run long commands (a build, a suite) in the background with a log under your tree's `tmp/`, and poll the log (`references/session.md`). Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing.
- Before you design a change to the library, study how the library already does the same kind of thing, and follow its way (`references/library.md`).
- Do not claim credit for the revival anywhere in a committed file. If git does not record who wrote something, reconstruct the authorship from the history. Do not guess it.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote. Do not commit scratch, such as logs and captured output. Do not rename a file to get it past `.gitignore`. The patch, report and programs of a probe that your brief asks for are not scratch (`references/committing.md`).
- End your work with a report. List in it the defects that you found, your decisions, and the points that your brief asks for. Put a question for the curator in it as a decision not taken (`references/records.md`).

## The parts

Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words that you need to understand what the query prints.

The parts, in the order that work meets them:

- Setting up each call, building, the caches, what to rebuild after an edit: `references/build-and-caches.md`
- The Bash tool and its timeout, long commands and polling, waits and the prompt cache, stopping processes, interrupts and stops of the session's process, the automatic permission check: `references/session.md`
- The base and its build, worktrees seeded from it, the old code beside the new: `references/worktrees.md`
- The build failing, JDKs, scalac and ASM traps, generated sources: `references/toolchain.md`
- The interpreter area: walk's code (`interpreter/`), where a fix of walk belongs, its checks at load, its natives, running programs under walk, the microGPT check: `references/interpreter.md`
- The compiled area: the checker, the code generator, the runtime, compiled runs, the `fortress` commands, the checker's time after a change: `references/compiler.md`
- The library area (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`): `references/library.md`
- The specification area (`Specification/`), Appendix I, citing it: `references/specification.md`
- How revived Fortress differs from the team's Fortress and from the languages that you know: `references/revival-changes.md`
- Exploring: where to search, what to record and report, which choices are yours: `references/exploring.md`
- Writing a test: `.test` keys, `XXX` expected failures and their promotion, refusals at load, how a defect that you found is recorded: `references/tests-writing.md`
- Running one test, a few, or a whole suite, and when to run a whole suite; what runs outside the gate: `references/tests-running.md`
- The gate: what it runs and writes, the atomic runs, the ladder regression, comparing with an earlier run: `references/gate.md`
- Committing and pushing: `references/committing.md`
- What every report holds and where it goes, findings and points to report; POSITIONS, FACTS and the gap ledger; the queries of the record and when to run each; writing the ledger with `ledger.py`; the repository's history: `references/records.md`
- This cloud platform (the machine, the disk, the network, the platform's stops, the transcript backup, a lost container): the `cloud-container` skill.

A task usually needs several parts. Every task needs `records.md`, for its queries and its report. If a task reads or changes the original tree (its Java and Scala, the library, the tests or the specification), or reviews such a change, read `revival-changes.md` whole, after this file, before work. A task that only runs a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a commit does not need it, until it must read a failing test's source: then read it. For example, a fix of walk needs `revival-changes.md`, `build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `interpreter.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md` and `committing.md`. An edit of the library needs the same parts and `library.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress

This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. The team left three forms that disagree: the specification, walk with the interpreter's library, and the compiled path with the compiler's library. The rules below resolve them.

Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).

A sentence that cites a ledger row states a behaviour that is not settled: a known departure from a rule, or a case that the rules do not decide yet. Either can change, so do not assert it as correct in a plain test, one without the `XXX` prefix. Where the rules decide the case, an `XXX` test asserts their answer. Where they do not, a plain test asserts today's behaviour beside the row (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded"). A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.

## Traits and objects

**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.

**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. So where the Meet Rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads, several declarations that together cover the meet serve. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).

**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. The checker refuses such a redeclaration where an object reaches the method of a generic self-typed trait along two paths (row 1037; `compiler.md`, "The checker's gaps", gives the form). An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier, so a program that writes one does not compile (row 650).

**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk and the checker stop the search for a cover at the same limits, which `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", gives. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).

**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:

- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.

In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` at `X` runs, also from an arm of a conditional or a `case` expression, a function expression or a local function. One shape fails the JVM's verification when its class loads: a `typecase` with `self` in one arm and another value in the other (row 1070). The row's test returns `self` at `R`, the type that its trait's `comprises { R }` lists. In that arm, bind `self` at the returned type, as `do r: R = self; r end`. A compiled body that `T` gives one of its methods can call a method on a value of type `X`. For a generic object that lists `T` first in its `extends` clause, no test runs such a body, and it may fail when the class loads (row 1052).

When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. In two cases walk does not read `self` so, and its load check refuses the valid pair (row 999):

- `T` is self-typed only through another self-typed trait that it extends;
- `T`'s method has static parameters of its own.

## Numbers

**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** In the interpreter's library, seven are value objects (P-178): `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64`. `QQ` is a trait, and its values are the value object `Ratio` (P-166). Do not extend a number type in a program. Declare a program's own number type below `Number` (P-160). Such a type runs on both paths. Walk refuses an object below one of the seven at load, as `object Mine extends ZZ32`: 'Attempt to extend object type ZZ32'. The compiler's prelude declares no `QQ`, and still declares the other seven as traits that a type can extend (row 1003). usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md
  F-87+                  the entry, then each entry it points to and each entry
                         that points to it, each once, one level
  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or
                         POSITIONS-history.md, oldest first: the provenance line
                         of each change and the line it replaced
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full
                         stop; when no current title holds it, the entry one of
                         whose former titles (in FACTS-history.md) does, with a
                         line saying it was retitled
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
